tips: Read the opening two chapters carefully. The reader knows what Job never learns—that his suffering is not punishment—so the friends' speeches can be measured against what really happened.

Don't take every speech as true. Job's friends say many things that sound pious, but God says at the end that they "have not spoken of me the thing that is right" (Job 42:7). Read the long dialogue (chapters 3–31) as an argument, not a list of answers.
Notice that God's speeches (chapters 38–41) never explain Job's suffering. Instead they show Job who God is, and that encounter is what changes him.

looksBack.title: A patriarchal setting
looksBack.text: Job lives outside Israel in the land of Uz and offers sacrifices for his family himself (Job 1:1, 5), much like Abraham and the other patriarchs in Genesis.

looksAhead.title: The patience of Job
looksAhead.text: James holds Job up as an example: "Ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy" (James 5:11).

looksAhead.title: A living Redeemer
looksAhead.text: Job's cry "I know that my redeemer liveth" (Job 19:25) has long been read by Christians as a hope fulfilled in the risen Christ.

tips: Don't read it straight through like a story. It is a collection of 150 songs and prayers in five books (Psalms 1–41, 42–72, 73–89, 90–106, 107–150), each ending with a short burst of praise.

Learn to recognize the main kinds of psalms: laments that cry out in trouble (such as Psalm 13), thanksgivings, hymns of praise, royal psalms about the king, and wisdom psalms. Most laments turn toward trust before they end.
Read the titles when they are given. A title such as Psalm 51's connects the psalm to a moment in David's life that you can read about in 1 and 2 Samuel.

looksBack.title: David's life
looksBack.text: Several titles tie psalms to events in 1 and 2 Samuel, such as David fleeing from Saul in the cave (Psalm 57; 1 Samuel 22:1) and his repentance after Bathsheba (Psalm 51; 2 Samuel 12).

looksAhead.title: Jesus prays the psalms
looksAhead.text: On the cross Jesus cries out the opening of Psalm 22: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46; Psalm 22:1).

looksAhead.title: The Lord at God's right hand
looksAhead.text: Psalm 110:1 is one of the Old Testament verses most often quoted in the New Testament, for example by Jesus (Matthew 22:44) and Peter (Acts 2:34–35).

looksAhead.title: The rejected stone
looksAhead.text: "The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner" (Psalm 118:22) is applied to Jesus in Matthew 21:42 and 1 Peter 2:7.

tips: Start with chapters 1–9. These longer poems are a father's appeal to choose wisdom over folly, and they give the short sayings in chapters 10–31 their meaning.
Remember that a proverb is a general truth, not a guaranteed promise. "Train up a child in the way he should go" (Proverbs 22:6) describes how life usually works, not a formula that never fails.
Read a little at a time and look for themes that recur—speech, work and laziness, money, friendship, anger. Gathering verses on one topic is often more helpful than reading straight through.

looksBack.title: Solomon's wisdom
looksBack.text: Solomon asked God for wisdom (1 Kings 3:9–12) and "spake three thousand proverbs" (1 Kings 4:32).

looksAhead.title: Wisdom and Christ
looksAhead.text: Wisdom present with God at creation (Proverbs 8:22–31) is echoed in the New Testament's description of Christ, in whom "are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3; compare John 1:1–3).

looksAhead.title: Proverbs in the letters
looksAhead.text: New Testament writers quote Proverbs often, such as Proverbs 3:11–12 on the Lord's discipline in Hebrews 12:5–6 and Proverbs 3:34 in James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5.

tips: Learn the key word "vanity" (Ecclesiastes 1:2). The Hebrew word means a breath or vapor—something fleeting that cannot be grasped—rather than simply pride.
Notice the phrase "under the sun." The Preacher deliberately looks at life as it appears from the earth alone, and much of his despair comes from that limited view.
Read the book through to its ending before drawing conclusions. The final word is "Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man" (Ecclesiastes 12:13).

looksBack.title: The curse on the ground
looksBack.text: The Preacher's frustration with toil and death echoes the curse of Genesis 3:17–19: man was taken from the dust, and "unto dust shalt thou return."

looksAhead.title: Subject to vanity
looksAhead.text: Paul writes that "the creature was made subject to vanity" but will be "delivered from the bondage of corruption" (Romans 8:20–21), answering the Preacher's lament with hope.

looksAhead.title: Treasure that lasts
looksAhead.text: Jesus' teaching on storing up treasure in heaven rather than on earth (Matthew 6:19–21) speaks to the same problem of riches that cannot be kept.

tips: Read it as poetry, not a narrative. It is a series of love songs between a bride and her beloved, with a chorus of friends, and the speakers change without warning.
Track who is speaking. Many Bibles add headings; in the Hebrew the pronouns and word endings show whether the man or the woman is speaking.
Notice the repeated warning: "stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please" (Song of Solomon 2:7; 3:5; 8:4). The book celebrates love while urging patience about its timing.

looksBack.title: The goodness of marriage
looksBack.text: The joy of the lovers recalls God's creation of man and woman, who "shall be one flesh" (Genesis 2:23–25).

looksAhead.title: Christ and the church
looksAhead.text: Jewish readers have long read the Song as a picture of God's love for Israel, and Christians as a picture of Christ's love for the church, which Paul calls "a great mystery" (Ephesians 5:25–32).

looksAhead.title: The wedding of the Lamb
looksAhead.text: The Bible ends with a wedding image: the church as a bride prepared for her husband (Revelation 19:7–9; 21:2).
